walkthroughs.body_html:
Four factors: concentration, temperature, surface area and catalyst.

More particles or more energy = more successful collisions per second.

Catalysts provide a lower activation energy pathway.

They are not used up in the reaction.

Enzymes are biological catalysts.

Some reactions reach an equilibrium: forward rate = reverse rate.

Example: N2 + 3H2 to 2NH3 (Haber process).

Concentrations stay constant but reactions continue - dynamic equilibrium.

mcqs.q: How does a catalyst speed up a reaction?
options: It provides an alternative reaction pathway with a lower activation energy.
A catalyst lowers the activation energy of the original reaction pathway.
A catalyst gives extra kinetic energy to the reactant particles.
The forward reaction stops once the reverse reaction begins.

mcqs.q: At dynamic equilibrium, what is happening to the reactions?
options: The forward reaction stops once the reverse reaction begins.
Forward and reverse reactions continue at equal rates; concentrations remain constant.
Both reactions stop because the system has reached balance.
A catalyst gives extra kinetic energy to the reactant particles.

mcqs.q: Why does increasing temperature increase the rate of reaction significantly?
options: Particles collide much more frequently at higher temperature, which is the main reason for the rate increase.
Mainly because a much larger fraction of collisions have energy at least equal to the activation energy; collision frequency increases only slightly.
A catalyst gives extra kinetic energy to the reactant particles.
Higher temperature increases the concentration of the reactants.
